Chapter Six: Intersections of Struggle—Race, Class, and Empire
Sometimes, doesn’t it feel like the world’s problems are just a mess of tangled threads? They’re tough to pull apart, and even tougher to ignore.
After the chants and the energy of a protest fade away, there’s this quiet moment when people start to realize—our struggles aren’t happening in neat little boxes. It’s never just about race, or class, or where you’re from. It’s about how all these forces work together, shaping our lives in ways we can see... and in ways we sometimes can’t.
Picture a young worker, coming home exhausted after a double shift. She asks herself—why is her neighborhood always last in line for repairs? Why does her school seem to have less of everything? Why do the police hang around her block more than anywhere else?
She might not have all the answers, but she feels the weight of history pressing down. The lines between economic injustice and racial discrimination? They start to blur... and you can see how each one makes the other worse.
Throughout the book, stories like hers are woven together, showing us how all these systems—slavery’s legacy, colonial violence, the greed of unchecked capitalism—they don’t just exist side by side. They feed off each other, creating a web that’s hard to escape, especially if you’re already vulnerable.
Most people don’t realize just how deeply connected these systems are, or how often they rely on the same old tricks: divide and conquer, punish and profit.
The author brings in real-life examples from all over the world. In South Africa, ending apartheid didn’t magically erase economic inequality. In the U.S., the civil rights movement scored big legal wins, but poverty and segregation still stuck around. And in Palestine, fighting against occupation is also about resisting economic exploitation.
The details might change from place to place, but the patterns? They’re stubbornly familiar.
For a lot of folks, this understanding doesn’t arrive all at once. It builds, bit by bit. A teacher might notice her students of color get disciplined more, or miss out on advanced classes. A factory worker might realize his pay stays low because the rules are rigged for the wealthy.
Eventually, it clicks: the fight for justice can’t just zero in on one kind of oppression. It’s got to tackle all of them together.
Building these intersectional movements? It’s hard, no question. It takes real listening, a willingness to learn—and sometimes, to unlearn what you thought you knew.
It means recognizing that each person’s experience is shaped by more than one identity—race, gender, class, nationality, ability. And maybe most importantly, it means being ready to share power, and to let those most affected by injustice lead the way.
